openers.contamination-and-remediation: A field can look healthy and still hold lead, pesticides or spilled fuel. Soil contamination is the presence of human-made chemicals or other changes to the natural soil, a form of land degradation, and it arrives through mining, heavy industry, spills, leaking underground tanks, farm chemicals and waste disposal. Some contaminants, such as lead, mercury, zinc and cadmium, resist breakdown, while too much nitrogen and phosphorus washing off the land pollutes lakes and rivers. People meet these contaminants by swallowing soil or dust, eating food grown in it, touching it and breathing its vapors, and the damage to ecosystems starts with the soil's own chemistry and organisms. This chapter follows those harms, then the cleanup, from digging and walling in to bacteria, fungi and plants put to work.

soil-env-001.title: Soil contamination: when the ground holds what it should not
soil-env-001.text: In 2012 the member states of the European Union reported more than 2.5 million potentially contaminated sites. That is the scale of soil contamination, also called soil or land pollution: the presence in soil of human-made chemicals or other changes to the natural soil environment. It is one form of {{ref:soil-env-062}}. Most of it comes from industry, farm chemicals or poor waste disposal. The commonest chemicals are petroleum hydrocarbons, solvents, pesticides, {{ref:soil-env-018}} and the compounds described in {{ref:soil-env-199}}. The main worry is health. People meet contaminants by touching soil, eating plants grown in it, breathing its vapors, or drinking groundwater polluted from below. Yet soil is not defenseless. At low levels, contamination often falls within a soil's own capacity to treat waste. Soil organisms transform it, mainly through microbial enzymes, while organic matter and clay adsorb it. Overload that capacity, and soil life and soil function suffer. The worst cases are derelict soils, damaged so badly by industrial contamination or development that the land cannot be used safely or productively. Mapping such sites and cleaning them up is slow and costly. It calls on geology, hydrology, chemistry, computer modelling and mapping software, along with the site's pollution history. The problem is best known in North America and Europe, where many countries have legal frameworks for contaminated land; elsewhere regulation tends to be looser. Of the EU's potential sites, about 342 thousand had been identified, and mineral oil and toxic metals made up around 60% of the contamination. In China, sampling found about 100,000 square kilometers of cultivated land polluted. Add land irrigated with contaminated water or buried by solid waste, and that is one-tenth of its cultivable land.

soil-env-015.title: Nonpoint source pollution: many small leaks from a wide land
soil-env-015.text: The leading cause of water pollution in the United States has no single address. Nonpoint source pollution is diffuse pollution of water or air that does not come from one discrete source. It is often the sum of small amounts of contaminants gathered from a large area, unlike {{ref:soil-env-204}}, which comes from one source. It travels in {{ref:soil-water-019}}, precipitation, atmospheric deposition, drainage and seepage, which makes it hard to trace. Its water pollutants are sediment, nutrients, toxic chemicals and germs, from towns, farms, highways, forests, mines and marinas. Nitrogen leaching from fertilized fields is a typical example. Even a factory smokestack, a single source, becomes a nonpoint source where long-range transport scatters its fallout. Because this pollution stems from everyday acts such as fertilizing lawns and spraying pesticides, it is hard to regulate. Towns fight it with grass buffer strips that let soil absorb pollutants, retention ponds where contaminants settle, porous pavement and constructed wetlands. In the United States, the chief culprits are farm runoff and hydromodification, the altering of how water flows.

soil-env-019.title: Nutrient pollution: fertilizer that feeds the wrong water
soil-env-019.text: The nitrogen and phosphorus that crops fail to use do not vanish. They leave the field and degrade the air and the water downstream. Nutrient pollution is water pollution caused by too many nutrients, usually nitrogen or phosphorus, entering water bodies. It is a primary cause of {{ref:soil-env-020}}. In lakes, rivers and coastal waters, the excess feeds a surge of algae. Sources include farm runoff, septic tank waste, feedlots, emissions from burning fuels and raw sewage. Much of it is nonpoint source pollution, spread thin over a landscape. The two nutrients travel differently. Many forms of phosphorus cling to soil particles, so phosphorus reaches water mostly through soil erosion. Nitrate moves mainly in water passing through the soil, such as interflow and tile drainage. Excess nitrogen also drives harmful algal blooms, oxygen-starved water, acid rain, nitrogen saturation in forests and climate change. People feel the effects directly. Excess nitrate in drinking water causes blue baby syndrome, water treatment can create harmful disinfection by-products, and swimming in algal blooms brings rashes and breathing problems. The bill is large too: higher water treatment costs, losses to commercial fishing, shellfish and recreational fishing, and lost tourism income. Remedies include vegetated buffer zones, constructed wetlands and vegetated ditches on farms, better wastewater treatment, and permits based on the polluter pays principle.

soil-env-012.title: Soil remediation: dig it up, treat it or wall it in
soil-env-012.text: Before contaminated land is redeveloped, it may first have to be cleaned. Soil remediation is that cleanup: removing, treating or containing pollutants to restore the soil's functions and values. Planning starts with field measurements of soil chemicals and with computer models of how those chemicals move and change. Every method falls on one side of a line. Ex situ methods excavate soil or pump groundwater for treatment at the surface. In situ methods treat the contamination where it lies. The traditional approaches are digging soil out for landfill and 'pump and treat' of groundwater. Excavation even extends to dredging contaminated bay muds and canals. Physical options include aerating soil on site, at the risk of air pollution, or heating it so contaminants turn to vapor and can be drawn off. Living things offer another route. Microbes, plants such as willow and fungi can break contaminants down or take up toxic metals, as {{ref:soil-env-023}} explains. Other in situ tools include solidifying and stabilizing the soil, reactive barriers that treat passing groundwater, chemical oxidation, and heating in place. Sometimes the answer is to leave the pollution and contain it. Barrier walls such as slurry walls must be impermeable and resist attack by the waste for their whole lifespan. Cleanup follows regulations. Where no standards exist, or they are only advisory, it rests on assessments of health and ecological risk.

soil-env-023.title: Bioremediation: putting microbes to work on pollution
soil-env-023.text: After the 2010 Gulf of Mexico oil spill, bacteria and archaea that could live on petroleum helped restore the coast. They used the oil as a source of both carbon and energy. That is bioremediation: using organisms, living or dead, to remove pollutants from soil, water, air and other media. The usual workers are bacteria, microalgae, fungi or plants. The method exploits their natural ability to absorb, accumulate and degrade pollutants, building on the living world of {{ref:soil-bio-011}}. It aims to be more sustainable, cheaper and more scalable than physical and chemical treatment. Most bioremediation is inadvertent, done by native organisms without help. Research focuses on speeding it up by inoculating sites with organisms or supplying nutrients. Chemically, most of these processes are redox reactions. An added electron acceptor, usually oxygen, oxidizes pollutants such as hydrocarbons, making them more soluble in water and easier to degrade. In the end, biodegradation turns hydrocarbons into carbon dioxide and water. Alternatively, an added electron donor reduces pollutants such as nitrate, perchlorate and chlorinated solvents. Toxic metals mark the hard limit. They cannot be biodegraded, only oxidized or reduced, so bioremediation offers few solutions for them. Techniques work in situ, at the site itself, or ex situ, on excavated material. They range from pumping air into soil to heaping dug soil in aerated piles, and plants can join in, as {{ref:soil-env-037}} shows. The main challenge is rate. The processes are slow.

soil-env-037.title: Phytoremediation: plants as slow, green cleanup crews
soil-env-037.text: A poplar tree can work as a pump. It draws water up through its roots and out through the plant, slowing the downward drift of soluble contaminants towards groundwater. This biological hydraulic containment is one face of phytoremediation: using living plants to clean up contaminated soil, air and water, a type of bioremediation. Plants can pull pollutants into their tissues, lock them in place, release them into the air or filter them from water. Plants and the microbes around their roots can also break pollutants down. Salt-tolerant plants called halophytes can extract salt from saline soil, and growing them reduces sodium carbonate in alkali soils. Breeding and genetic engineering can help. Tobacco given a bacterial nitroreductase gene removed the explosive TNT faster and resisted its toxicity. Bacteria in the {{ref:soil-bio-143}} speed metals into the roots of plants that hoard them, by producing chelating or dissolving agents. For all its promise, phytoremediation has never been used at large scale, and microbial bioremediation has so far done better.

soil-env-018.title: Heavy metals: the contaminants that never break down
soil-env-018.text: Within 1.1 km of the Sudbury nickel-copper smelter in Canada, soil held up to 5,104 ppm nickel and 2,892 ppm copper. Nearby plants carried nickel, copper and aluminium too. Heavy metals in soil are metals such as lead, mercury, zinc and cadmium that resist breakdown and rank among the commonest soil contaminants. They come from sewage sludge, mining, vehicle exhaust, burning fuels, industry, landfills and some fertilizers. In China, heavy metals and metalloids contaminate 19% of agricultural soils, and some 12 million tonnes of grain are contaminated each year. Unlike organic pollutants, they cannot be degraded. Microbes can at best immobilize them, as when mobile uranium U(VI) is reduced to less mobile U(IV), an approach still more conceptual than practical. Iron, cobalt, copper and zinc are essential nutrients that turn toxic in larger amounts. Arsenic, cadmium, mercury and lead are highly poisonous. Even the name is disputed. Definitions cover up to 96 elements, and IUPAC calls the term meaningless and misleading, yet it remains widely used in science.

soil-env-033.title: Mycoremediation: fungi that digest what bacteria cannot
soil-env-033.text: In creosote-soaked soils rich in {{ref:soil-env-199}}, fungi have proven the most successful way to stop the pollution spreading. Mycoremediation is a form of bioremediation that uses fungi to decontaminate the environment. Their menu is long: heavy metals, organic pollutants, dyes, petroleum fuels, pharmaceuticals, pesticides and herbicides. Fungal enzymes are non-specific, so they break down substances that bacteria degrade poorly, such as the drug paracetamol and fragrances. The method needs no expensive equipment. That suits small jobs such as filtering household wastewater or industrial effluent through fungi. Cold-tolerant Antarctic fungi degrade petroleum where removing contaminated soil would be costly. Acid- and radiation-resistant species may help treat radioactive waste. In burnt forests, pellets of fungal spores coated in agarose can break down toxins and stimulate regrowth. Even the by-products have value, from enzymes such as laccase to edible and medicinal mushrooms.

soil-env-009.title: How contamination ripples from soil chemistry up the food chain
soil-env-009.text: The thickness of a forest floor can betray a poisoned soil. The ecological effects of soil contamination begin with changes to soil chemistry and to the organisms living in the soil. Many hazardous chemicals change soil chemistry radically even at low concentrations, altering the metabolism of soil microbes and animals. Wiping out part of the base of the {{ref:soil-bio-025}} can have major consequences for predators and other consumers. Earthworms and other soil ecosystem engineers are very sensitive to contaminants. As they decline, the humus form shifts from mull, with good crumb structure, to undecayed mor over compact soil. So a quick look at forest-floor thickness and the mineral horizon below has been proposed as a cheap early check for contamination. On farmland, heavy metals and metalloids alter plant metabolism and often cut yields. The weakened crops then shield the soil less from erosion. Some contaminants have long half-lives, and others decay into derivative chemicals that are contaminants themselves.

soil-env-007.title: How soil contaminants find their way into people
soil-env-007.text: Some studies estimate that 90% of human exposure to soil contaminants comes from eating contaminated food. Exposure pathways are the routes by which those contaminants reach people: swallowing soil or dust, eating food grown in it, skin contact, and breathing its vapors or dust. Most exposure is accidental. Toxic metals climb the food chain through plants growing in metal-rich soils, which tends to lead to pollution-related diseases. A potentially greater threat lies underground. Contaminants can seep into aquifers used for irrigation or drinking, sometimes far from any visible source, a pattern called long-range diffuse soil contamination. Even soil's defenses can backfire. Organic matter and clay adsorb contaminants, but as suspended colloids, tiny particles adrift in water, they can also carry them down into the subsurface.

soil-env-004.title: Pesticides: most of the spray misses its target
soil-env-004.text: More than 98% of sprayed insecticides and 95% of herbicides end up somewhere other than their target, including the air, water and soil. Pesticides are chemical or biological agents used to kill pests such as weeds, insects and fungi, and they are a major class of soil contaminant. Herbicides are the most common type, at about 50% of all pesticide use worldwide. Soil bacteria break down most herbicides, and they quickly turn glyphosate into a compound called AMPA. Yet glyphosate residues still turn up in drinking water, farm produce and food. The herbicides 2,4-D and 2,4,5-T can carry dioxin as an impurity, lethal even at low concentrations. Paraquat, banned in the EU, is highly toxic and lingers because clay lattices adsorb and protect it. Synthetic insecticides form three main groups. There are persistent organochlorines, described in {{ref:soil-env-005}}, organophosphates that block nerve transmission, and neonicotinoids that act on the insect central nervous system. Neonicotinoid residues have risen greatly with heavy use, and they harm pollinators as well as pests.

soil-env-002.title: Where soil contaminants come from, from tyres to coal ash
soil-env-002.text: In areas industrialized before about 1960, a common source of soil contamination was ash from coal burned for heating and ore smelting. Coal concentrates arsenic, cadmium, lead and zinc, and burning leaves all but the mercury in the ash. The ash also carries {{ref:soil-env-199}}, known human carcinogens whose acceptable soil levels typically range from 0.1 mg/kg to 10 mg/kg depending on the compound. Sources of soil contamination are the activities and materials that put contaminants into soil. They include mining and heavy industry, spills, leaking underground storage tanks and agrochemicals. Lead-based paint, nuclear waste, sewage, landfills and electronic waste add more. Road traffic adds lead from exhaust and cadmium and zinc from tyre wear, and some rocks are naturally rich in toxic elements. Treated sewage sludge, or biosolids, is a controversial fertilizer. It is rich in nitrogen, phosphate and potassium, but generally carries more organisms, pesticides and heavy metals than other soil. In vineyards and orchards, repeated fungicide sprays build up copper, even on organic farms.

soil-env-020.title: Eutrophication: when nutrients smother a lake
soil-env-020.text: Every summer a mass of oxygen-starved bottom water forms where the Mississippi River enters the Gulf of Mexico. This dead zone is comparable in area to New Jersey. It is a product of eutrophication. That is the build-up of nutrients in a body of water, boosting algae and other organisms that may then use up its oxygen. Eutrophication can be natural, a slow build-up of sediment and nutrients over geological time. Or it can be cultural, when sewage, industrial wastewater and fertilizer runoff release nutrients, the nutrient pollution of the last entries. Which nutrient matters depends on the water. Phosphorus usually limits plant growth in fresh water, and nitrogen in the sea. So excess phosphorus fuels the problem in lakes, and excess nitrogen in marine waters. The sequence is grim. Algal blooms shade out plants on the bottom. When the algae die, bacteria decomposing them use up the oxygen, and fish and invertebrates die. Severe blooms called red tides release toxins as they die and can leave dead zones with no life at all. The problem grew with chemical fertilizers in the mid-1900s green revolution. Since phosphate detergents were phased out in the 1970s, sewage and agriculture dominate phosphate inputs. Prevention means cutting nutrients from sewage, farms and other sources. Shellfish and seaweed can also take up nitrogen and so curb cyanobacterial blooms.

soil-env-199.title: PAHs: soot-born rings that cling to carbon
soil-env-199.text: Across 76 sites in London's urban soils, the 16 parent PAHs ranged from 4 to 67 mg/kg of dry soil, averaging 18 mg/kg. Most were four- to six-ring forms from combustion. A polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon, or PAH, is an organic compound made of several fused aromatic rings, formed mostly by incomplete burning of organic matter. Sources include engine exhaust, incinerators, forest fires, coal, petroleum, oil spills and creosote. Burning moorland vegetation adds PAHs to the peat surface. Light two- and three-ring forms spread widely, dissolved in water or as gases. Heavier ones ride on particles and settle more locally. PAHs have a strong affinity for organic carbon, so organic-rich sediments are substantial sinks. Unlike many long-lived pollutants, PAHs do not concentrate up food chains, because most vertebrates metabolize and excrete them fairly quickly. Exposure is linked to cancers. The EU and US EPA regulate PAHs in air, water and soil, with benzo[a]pyrene the usual marker compound.

soil-env-198.title: Persistent organic pollutants: the chemicals that reach the poles
soil-env-198.text: Chemicals never used in Antarctica or the Arctic turn up there anyway. Persistent organic pollutants, or POPs, are toxic organic compounds that resist chemical, biological and light-driven breakdown and persist in the environment. Most are pesticides or insecticides. Others are solvents, pharmaceuticals and industrial chemicals, and only a few arise naturally, as from volcanoes and forest fires. They are typically halogenated, and their carbon-chlorine bonds resist being split by water or light. They dissolve poorly in water but readily in oils and fats, and solid particles capture them easily. That fat solubility lets them build up in fatty tissue. They volatilize from soils, vegetation and water, travel long distances in air and settle again. Indoors, levels in air and dust often exceed those in outdoor air and soil. The 2001 Stockholm Convention named a 'dirty dozen', including aldrin, chlordane, dieldrin, DDT, PCBs and dioxins, and newer POPs such as PFOS have been added since. Efforts focus more on banning their production and use worldwide than on removing them from the environment.

soil-env-005.title: DDT, the cheap insecticide that never quite left
soil-env-005.text: In 1970 the world used 72,000 tonnes of DDT. It was a cheap, potent and persistent organochlorine insecticide, used on a massive scale from the 1930s. DDT turned up worldwide in fish and birds and even in Antarctic snow. Barely soluble in water but very soluble in fats, it thins birds' eggshells. It is blamed for the 1950s decline of ospreys and peregrine falcons, which are now recovering. The Stockholm Convention banned it in 2001. In 2006 the World Health Organization allowed it back only for controlling vector-borne diseases in some tropical countries. In soil it lingers. Soils and sediments soak it up, then act as long-term sources of exposure. Its half-life in soil is 2 to 15 years, though depending on conditions it can range from 22 days to 30 years. Aerobic and anaerobic microbes break it down, but its products DDE and DDD are just as persistent. A 2018 study still found residues in European soils and Spanish rivers, and people carry levels 5 to 10 times lower than in the 1970s.

soil-env-016.title: Farm runoff: the diffuse pollution of the countryside
soil-env-016.text: Ploughing a large tract exposes and loosens buried soil. The next storm erodes it more easily and carries more fertilizer and pesticide into nearby water. That is agricultural nonpoint source pollution: diffuse pollution of water by nutrients, agrochemicals and sediment washed or carried off farmland. Nitrogen and phosphorus arrive as {{ref:soil-fert-001}}, manure, wastewater or sludge. They also enter runoff from crop residues, irrigation water, wildlife and atmospheric deposition. Pesticides such as DDT or atrazine travel through waterways or drift on the wind as spray. Farmers have many controls: contour ploughing, mulching, crop rotation, perennial crops, riparian buffers, conservation tillage, nutrient management plans and integrated pest management.

soil-env-026.title: Natural attenuation: letting a site clean itself, under watch
soil-env-026.text: Sometimes the best cleanup crew is already in the ground. Natural attenuation is the breakdown of contaminants by a site's own microbes, with no human intervention, though the site must still be monitored. It is one of the broad categories of bioremediation, beside feeding the native microbes and adding new ones. Time helps in other ways too. Contaminants can become less bioavailable, harder for living things to take up, while microbes and whole ecosystems adapt to them. Monitored natural attenuation is one technique for remediating derelict soils, alongside leaching, air sparging, soil conditioners, phytoremediation and other bioremediation. Stepping in can even backfire. Where reducing conditions favor anaerobic bacteria, injecting oxygen to speed aerobic attenuation can suppress the anaerobic kind.

soil-env-011.title: Why the same pollutant harms one soil and spares another
soil-env-011.text: The same amount of a contaminant can be toxic in one soil and harmless in another. Heavy metals and other contaminants disrupt soil functions, such as the cycling of carbon and nitrogen, by altering the activity, mix and numbers of soil microorganisms. How much harm they do depends on the soil. Its pH, organic matter content and texture strongly modify how mobile, bioavailable and toxic a pollutant is. Over time, natural attenuation can make contaminants less available, and microbes and ecosystems can adapt. So risk assessment and remediation must be soil-specific.

soil-env-008.title: What soil contaminants do to the human body
soil-env-008.text: At high enough doses, many soil contaminants can kill through contact, inhalation or ingestion. Most harm is slower. The health effects of soil contamination vary with the pollutant, the route of exposure and how vulnerable the exposed people are. Long exposure to chromium, lead and other metals, petroleum, solvents and many pesticides can cause cancer, birth defects or other chronic disease. Benzene at sufficient concentrations is linked to leukemia, mercury and cyclodienes to kidney damage, and PCBs and cyclodienes to liver toxicity. Nitrate and ammonia from livestock manure are hazards in soil and groundwater too.

soil-env-006.title: The poisoned ground that wars leave behind
soil-env-006.text: Along the former World War I front in Belgium and France, abandoned sites where munitions were dismantled are still contaminated with arsenic and lead. War-related soil contamination is pollution left by munitions, chemical agents and other agents of war. Disposal of munitions, and careless manufacture under wartime urgency, can contaminate soil for long periods. Mustard gas stored in World War II contaminated some sites for up to 50 years. Anthrax weapon tests left Gruinard island quarantined for 48 years. Little is published on the subject, largely because governments restrict publication of material related to the war effort.
